content.purpose: Get back to a prompt when a command will not finish on its own.
content.mentalModel: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D look similar and do completely different things. Ctrl+C sends an interrupt signal to whatever is running, asking it to stop. Ctrl+D sends nothing at all: it closes the input stream, so a program reading input sees that there is no more. When the shell itself sees end of input, it has nothing left to read and exits, which is why Ctrl+D at a prompt logs you out.

demonstration.explanation: Waits five minutes and gives you no prompt back. Press Ctrl+C and it stops immediately.
With no file, cat reads what you type and echoes it back. Ctrl+C abandons it; Ctrl+D tells it the input has ended, which is the tidier way out.

remember: Ctrl+D means end of input, and at a prompt that ends your shell session
A command that gives no prompt back is usually waiting, not broken
dangerous: Ctrl+C stops a command part-way, which can leave a half-written file behind

tasks.instruction: Run sleep 300 and notice you do not get a prompt back. Press Ctrl+C to interrupt it. Then confirm you are back in control by creating a file called interrupted.txt.

validators.message: sleep 300 is still running, so it was not interrupted. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

hints: The command has not failed; it is doing exactly what you asked and waiting.
Ctrl+C sends an interrupt to the running command.

tasks.instruction: Use cat with no file name to type two lines of your own into typed.txt, then end the input properly rather than interrupting it. If you use Ctrl+C instead of Ctrl+D the file will be empty.

validators.message: typed.txt has fewer than two lines. Ctrl+C abandons cat before it writes; Ctrl+D closes the input so what you typed is saved.

hints: cat with no arguments reads from your keyboard. You can redirect that into a file.
Type two lines, then press Ctrl+D on an empty line to signal end of input.

reviewQuestions.question: You are at an empty prompt and press Ctrl+D. What happens?
answers: The shell sees end of input and your session ends
Nothing, because no command is running
reviewQuestions.explanation: Ctrl+D is end of input, not a cancel. With no more input to read, the shell exits.

reviewQuestions.question: A command has been running for a minute and printed nothing. What is the most likely explanation?
answers: It is working or waiting, and has not finished yet
reviewQuestions.explanation: No prompt means the command has not exited. A command that does not exist reports so immediately.
